subject.title: Smoke
subject.author: Théophile Gautier
subject.text:
Over there, trees are sheltering
A hunchedback hut... A slum, no more...
Roof askew, walls and wainscoting
Falling away... Moss hides the door.
 
Only one shutter, hanging... But
Seeping over the windowsill,
Like frosted breath, proof that this hut,
This slum, is living, breathing still.
 
Corkscrew of smoke... A wisp of blue
Escapes the hovel, whose soul it is...
Rises to God himself, and who
Receives the news and makes it his.

title: The Poem That Breaks the Rule Its Own Book Ends On
standfirst: Théophile Gautier's Émaux et Camées closes on a manifesto ordering poets to fight hard, resistant material — marble, bronze, agate — because only that survives. Twenty-seven poems earlier, in twelve of the softest lines he ever published, a soul reaches God as nothing but smoke escaping a crack in a wall.

sections.heading: The Corkscrew and the Wisp
sections.body:
*Fumée* spends its first two stanzas refusing to say its own title. A roof leans, a wall crumbles, moss covers the threshold, a single shutter hangs over a blocked window — architecture in decay, sized up from the outside, the way you'd size up a ruin before deciding whether anyone still lives there. Only in the seventh line does the poem move. Norman Shapiro's translation calls what escapes the hut "a corkscrew of smoke," an odd, almost mechanical image for something with no shape at all, and a faithful one: Gautier's own word is [*tire-bouchon*](https://www.poetica.fr/poeme-2581/theophile-gautier-fumee/), literally corkscrew, the same tool you'd use on a bottle.

Where the translation quietly drifts is the last line. Gautier's French says only that the smoke, turning its thin blue thread, [carries news to God](https://www.poetica.fr/poeme-2581/theophile-gautier-fumee/) of the soul shut inside the hovel — a message crossing a distance. Shapiro's English has the smoke "Rises to God himself," who "Receives the news and makes it his" — a small escalation, from a report delivered to a soul actually claimed. Something had to close the rhyme that Gautier's French didn't need to close, and the choice is defensible. But it changes what the poem's last line is actually asserting.

sections.heading: A Small Poem in a Book That Kept Growing
sections.body:
Émaux et Camées — Enamels and Cameos — [first appeared in 1852 with eighteen poems](https://essentiels.bnf.fr/fr/article/7f33f3ba-6a30-4154-a29f-88c254a924ae-emaux-et-camees). Gautier kept adding to it for the rest of his life, through four expanding editions, until [the definitive edition of 1872](https://essentiels.bnf.fr/fr/article/7f33f3ba-6a30-4154-a29f-88c254a924ae-emaux-et-camees) — the year he died — ran to fifty-three. In the modern collected ordering, *Fumée* sits as [the twentieth poem of forty-seven](https://fr.wikisource.org/wiki/%C3%89maux_et_Cam%C3%A9es), on page 64 of a book that runs to 132 — closer to the middle than to either end, filed between an ode after Anacreon and a poem called Apollonie. Exactly when Gautier wrote it, or which of the book's four editions first carried it, isn't clear from the sources available here.

A Nadar portrait from around 1856 catches him partway through that two-decade revision — mid-career, already the public face of the doctrine the book would eventually close on.

sections.heading: Sculpt, File, Chisel
sections.body:
The rule the book is remembered for comes right at its close. *L'Art* [first ran in the journal L'Artiste in 1857](https://essentiels.bnf.fr/fr/article/7f33f3ba-6a30-4154-a29f-88c254a924ae-emaux-et-camees) before Gautier folded it into later editions of Émaux et Camées, where it now closes the book as its manifesto. Its argument, in short, clipped stanzas, is that soft material makes soft art. "Statuaire, repousse / L'argile que pétrit / Le pouce" — sculptor, reject the clay a thumb kneads — [because clay yields too easily](https://www.poetica.fr/poeme-454/theophile-gautier-art/) and lets the mind wander while the hand works. Fight instead with material that resists: Carrara and Paros marble, bronze cast in Syracuse, a vein of agate. The poem's best-known line states the stakes outright — "Tout passe. — L'art robuste / Seul a l'éternité," everything passes, only robust art has eternity — and follows it with what that has meant in practice: statues that outlive the cities they stood in, a coin a farmer turns up that outlives the emperor stamped on it. The instruction that closes the poem, and the book, is four words: sculpt, file, chisel.

The same year "L'Art" first appeared, Charles Baudelaire dedicated *Les Fleurs du Mal* to Gautier, calling him, [in the dedication's own words](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Les_Fleurs_du_mal), the perfect magician of French letters. By 1857, the doctrine of hard, resistant art already had serious admirers.

sections.heading: The Rule This Poem Doesn't Follow
sections.body: *Fumée* does none of what *L'Art* instructs. No marble, no bronze, no resistance offered or overcome. Its central image is smoke — about as far from a resistant material as language has a word for, defined by refusing shape, dispersing as soon as it forms. Gautier doesn't fight it, doesn't fix it, doesn't even work it into the kind of hard enamel the book takes its name from. He just lets it turn and rise. If "L'Art" insists that only robust art reaches eternity, "Fumée" quietly stages the opposite case twenty-seven poems earlier: a soul reaching God on nothing sturdier than breath finding a gap in a wall. Nothing in the record suggests Gautier meant the two poems to argue with each other — they were written years apart, for a book he kept revising until the year he died — but read back to back, in the order he eventually settled on, the softest poem in Émaux et Camées sits closer to its centre than its famous, hardest one, which he saved for last.

sections.heading: The Cost of Useless Art
sections.body: Gautier's manifesto insisted that art should serve nothing beyond itself. His own working life did not allow for that. [From 1836 to 1855 he was a weekly contributor to La Presse and Le Moniteur Universel](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Theophile-Gautier), took editorial posts at Revue de Paris in 1851 and L'Artiste in 1856, and wrote for periodicals beyond those. He complained that journalism was draining off the creative energy his poetry needed, and kept doing it anyway, because the writing paid for two mistresses, his three children, and his two sisters. Only late in life did [Princess Mathilde Bonaparte give him a sinecure post as a librarian](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Theophile-Gautier) to ease the strain. He died on 23 October 1872, at Neuilly-sur-Seine, aged sixty-one — the same year the book he'd spent two decades revising reached its final form.

sections.heading: How a Minor Poem Crosses a Language
sections.body: *Fumée* is not one of the poems Émaux et Camées is remembered for — not "Carmen," not "Symphonie en Blanc Majeur." It exists in English mostly because [Norman Shapiro, a professor of Romance languages at Wesleyan University](https://yalebooks.yale.edu/book/9780300181555/selected-lyrics/), decided the whole book was worth doing, not just its anthology pieces. His *Selected Lyrics*, [published by Yale University Press](https://yalebooks.yale.edu/book/9780300181555/selected-lyrics/) in its Margellos World Republic of Letters series, puts the complete Émaux et Camées into English alongside selections from España and Gautier's earlier collections — dozens of short poems, this one included, that most readers would otherwise only meet in French, if they met them at all. It travelled the way its own last image describes: quietly, without ceremony, carrying something across a distance to whoever happens to be listening.
